media.title: What remainders do two numbers leave together?
media.context: We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: One number leaves remainder three when divided by seven, and another leaves five. Writing them with letters shows the remainders of their sum, their take away and their multiplication.

video_script.why: The child can multiply out two brackets, but has not yet used letters to follow remainders through a sum, a take away and a multiplication.

marks.ask: a question mark appears over the words sum, take away and multiplication
marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.first: the first number card, leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7, appears
marks.second: the second number card, leaves remainder 5 when divided by 7, appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='first'/>A number leaves a remainder of three when divided by seven,
<bookmark mark='second'/>and another number leaves a remainder of five when divided by seven.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the remainder when their sum, difference, and product are divided by seven?
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; two number cards: leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7, and leaves remainder 5 when divided by 7; a question mark over sum, take away, multiplication

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the two number cards stay on the board

marks.groups: groups of seven counters are shown with three counters left over
marks.second: a second set of groups with five left over is labelled 7b + 5

beats.colours: the groups of seven in one colour, the leftovers in another
narration: <bookmark mark='groups'/>Divide by seven.
Some full groups of seven are made, and a few are left over.
<bookmark mark='first'/>The first number is seven times eigh, plus three.
<bookmark mark='second'/>The second is seven times b, plus five.
beats.on_screen: a row of 7 counters repeated three times with 3 left over, labelled 7a + 3; a row of 7 counters repeated four times with 5 left over, labelled 7b + 5

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers seven eigh plus three, and seven b plus five.
beats.on_screen: Given: the numbers 7a + 3 and 7b + 5

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the remainders of their sum, take away and multiplication.
beats.on_screen: To find: the remainder of their sum, take away and multiplication when divided by 7

marks.out: 8 is split as 7 + 1, and 7(a + b + 1) + 1 is written
marks.rem: the 1 left after the bracket is marked as the remainder

beats.colours: the multiples of 7 in one colour, the remainder in another
narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step one, the sum.
Seven eigh plus three plus seven b plus five is seven eigh plus seven b plus eight.
<bookmark mark='out'/>Eight is seven plus one.
Seven comes out of three parts, giving seven times eigh plus b plus one, plus one.
<bookmark mark='rem'/>The remainder is one.

marks.rem: 7(b - a) + 2 is written, with 2 marked as the remainder
marks.five: -2 is written as -7 + 5, giving 7(a - b - 1) + 5, with 5 marked as the remainder

beats.colours: the multiples of 7 in one colour, the remainder in another
narration: <bookmark mark='take'/>Step two, the take away.
Seven b plus five, minus seven eigh plus three, is seven b minus seven eigh plus two.
<bookmark mark='rem'/>That is seven times b minus eigh, plus two.
The remainder is two.
<bookmark mark='back'/>Taken the other way round, we get seven times eigh minus b, minus two.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Minus two is minus seven plus five.
The remainder is five.
beats.on_screen: Take away: (7b + 5) - (7a + 3) = 7b - 7a + 2 = 7(b - a) + 2. The other way round: (7a + 3) - (7b + 5) = 7(a - b) - 2 = 7(a - b - 1) + 5

marks.all: 49ab + 35a + 21b + 15 is written as the whole expansion

beats.colours: the four parts in the accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step three, the multiplication.
Every term meets every term.
Seven eigh times seven b is forty nine eigh b.
Seven eigh times five is thirty five eigh.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Three times seven b is twenty one b.
Three times five is fifteen.
<bookmark mark='all'/>We get forty nine eigh b plus thirty five eigh plus twenty one b plus fifteen.
beats.on_screen: Multiplication: (7a + 3)(7b + 5) = 49ab + 35a + 21b + 15

marks.sum: 22 = 21 + 1 is written and ticked, and 12 - 10 = 2 is written and ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='pick'/>Step four, put the answers back in the question, with numbers from the book.
Take eigh as twenty three and b as twenty seven.
The numbers are one hundred sixty four and one hundred ninety four.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Their sum is three hundred fifty eight, which is seven times fifty one, plus one.
Their difference is thirty, which is seven times four, plus two.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Their product is thirty one thousand eight hundred sixteen.
That is seven times four thousand five hundred forty five, plus one.
<bookmark mark='group'/>Fifteen is fourteen plus one, so seven comes out of the rest.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The sum leaves remainder one, the take away leaves two, and the multiplication leaves one.
beats.on_screen: Answer: sum, remainder 1; take away, remainder 2 (or 5 the other way round); multiplication: 49ab + 35a + 21b + 15 = 7(7ab + 5a + 3b + 2) + 1, remainder 1

video_script.anchor: the two numbers of the book's question, one leaving remainder three and one leaving remainder five when divided by seven
video_script.design: One idea: write each number as seven times a whole number plus its remainder, and pull seven out of the working. The two numbers stay on the board. The last regrouping, for the multiplication, is left until the answer.
source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 6)
maths_rules: take away: (7b + 5) − (7a + 3) = 7b − 7a + 2 = 7(b − a) + 2, remainder 2; the other way round (7a + 3) − (7b + 5) = 7(a − b) − 2 = 7(a − b − 1) + 5, remainder 5
video_script.payoff_line: The sum leaves remainder one, the take away leaves two, and the multiplication leaves one.

final_answer.value: Sum: remainder 1; difference: remainder 2 (or 5 the other way round); product: remainder 1
final_answer.spoken: the sum leaves remainder one, the take away leaves two, and the multiplication leaves one

video_script.substitution: Write each number as seven times a whole number plus its remainder, then multiply out the way the cards in the book did.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: write each number as seven times something plus its remainder, then multiply out and pull seven out of what is left. Watch for students who add or multiply the remainders and stop, forgetting that the result can be larger than seven.

interaction_points.answer: Sum: remainder 1; difference: remainder 2 (or 5 the other way round); product: remainder 1

media.context: We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Three numbers in a row are chosen, the middle one is squared, and the multiplication of the other two is taken away. Examples show a pattern, and letters prove it for every set.

video_script.why: The child can multiply out two brackets, but has not yet used letters to explain a pattern seen in sets of numbers.

marks.mid: the middle tile is squared, 6 x 6, beside the row
marks.row: three number tiles 5, 6 and 7 appear in a row
marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.ends: the two outer tiles are joined by a multiplication, 5 x 7

beats.colours: the middle tile in one colour, the outer tiles in another
narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='row'/>Choose three consecutive numbers, square the middle one,
<bookmark mark='mid'/>and subtract the product of the other two.
<bookmark mark='ends'/>Repeat the same with other sets of numbers.
What pattern do you notice?
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; three number tiles 5, 6, 7 in a row; the middle tile squared, 6 x 6, and the other two multiplied, 5 x 7

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the three tiles stay on the board

marks.arrows: an arrow one step left of the middle tile is marked -1, and an arrow one step right is marked +1
marks.letters: the three tiles are relabelled n - 1, n and n + 1

beats.colours: the -1 arrow and the +1 arrow in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='arrows'/>The number before the middle one is one less.
The number after it is one more.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>Call the middle number n.
The three numbers are n minus one, n, and n plus one.
beats.on_screen: the three tiles relabelled n - 1, n, n + 1, with arrows: one step left from n is -1, one step right is +1

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three numbers in a row.
beats.on_screen: Given: three numbers in a row, n - 1, n, n + 1

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the pattern, and why it holds.
beats.on_screen: To find: the pattern, and why it holds

narration: <bookmark mark='five'/>Step one, try some sets.
For five, six and seven, thirty six minus thirty five leaves one.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>For nine, ten and eleven, one hundred minus ninety nine leaves one.

marks.write: n² - (n - 1)(n + 1) is written as the same steps with letters

narration: <bookmark mark='write'/>Step two, write the same steps with letters.
The middle squared is n squared.
We take away n minus one times n plus one.

marks.sum: n - n = 0 is written, giving n² - 1
marks.more: the parts n and -n are written next to each other
marks.parts: n x n = n², n x 1 = n, -1 x n = -n and -1 x 1 = -1 are written as the four parts

beats.colours: the like terms in one colour
narration: <bookmark mark='parts'/>Step three, multiply out the brackets.
N times n is n squared, and n times one is n.
<bookmark mark='more'/>Minus one times n is minus n, and minus one times one is minus one.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Plus n and minus n cancel, so we are left with n squared minus one.

marks.put: n² - (n² - 1) is written, with the brackets around n² - 1

narration: <bookmark mark='put'/>Step four, put that in.
We have n squared, take away n squared minus one.
beats.on_screen: n² - (n² - 1)

marks.pick: n = 20 is chosen, and 19, 20, 21 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='pick'/>Step five, put the answer back in the question.
Take n as twenty three, so the numbers are twenty two, twenty three and twenty four.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Twenty three squared is five hundred twenty nine.
Twenty two times twenty four is five hundred twenty eight.
<bookmark mark='tick'/>Five hundred twenty nine minus five hundred twenty eight is one.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The answer is always one, for every set of three numbers in a row.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Taking n squared minus one away from n squared leaves one, whatever n is.
beats.on_screen: Answer: n² - (n - 1)(n + 1) = n² - (n² - 1) = 1, always

media.description: Two pairs of multiplications from the book are compared without multiplying them out. Each number is written as a middle number plus or minus a small step, so that a square is taken away from a square.

<bookmark mark='second2'/>That is two thousand five hundred minus five hundred seventy six.

In each pair, we start from the same number.

<bookmark mark='rule'/>Taking away the smaller number leaves more.

$1$. Another square: $3$, $4$ over $10$, $11$ gives $3 \times 11 = 33$ and $4 \times 10 = 40$; again $40 - 33 = 7$.

$3$. $a(a + 8) = a^2 + 8a$.
$4$. $(a + 1)(a + 7) = a^2 + 7a + a + 7 = a^2 + 8a + 7$.

Answer: The diagonal products always differ by $7$, because $(a + 1)(a + 7) - a(a + 8) = 7$

content.text: Verify which of the following statements are true. (i): $(k + 1)(k + 2) - (k + 3)$ is always $2$. (ii): $(2q + 1)(2q - 3)$ is a multiple of $4$. (iii): Squares of even numbers are multiples of $4$, and squares of odd numbers are $1$ more than multiples of $8$. (iv): $(6n + 2)^2 - (4n + 3)^2$ is $5$ less than a square number.
content.question: Verify which of the following statements are true. (i) (k + 1)(k + 2) − (k + 3) is always 2. (ii) (2q + 1)(2q − 3) is a multiple of 4. (iii) Squares of even numbers are multiples of 4, and squares of odd numbers are 1 more than multiples of 8. (iv) (6n + 2)² − (4n + 3)² is 5 less than a square number.

content.publication_text: Verify which of the following statements are true. (i): $(k + 1)(k + 2) - (k + 3)$ is always $2$. (ii): $(2q + 1)(2q - 3)$ is a multiple of $4$. (iii): Squares of even numbers are multiples of $4$, and squares of odd numbers are $1$ more than multiples of $8$. (iv): $(6n + 2)^2 - (4n + 3)^2$ is $5$ less than a square number.

content.text:
$1$. (i): $k^2 + 3k + 2 - k - 3 = k^2 + 2k - 1$; for $k = 1$ it is $2$ but for $k = 2$ it is $7$. False.
$2$. (ii): $4q^2 - 6q + 2q - 3 = 4q^2 - 4q - 3$, which is odd. False.
$3$. (iii): $(2m)^2 = 4m^2$, and $(2m + 1)^2 = 4m^2 + 4m + 1 = 4m(m + 1) + 1$; $m(m + 1)$ is even, so $4m(m + 1)$ is a multiple of $8$. True.
$4$. (iv): $36n^2 + 24n + 4 - (16n^2 + 24n + 9) = 20n^2 - 5$; $20n^2$ is not a square for $n = 1$. False.
Answer: (i): False (ii): False (iii): True (iv): False
steps: (i) k² + 3k + 2 − k − 3 = k² + 2k − 1; for k = 1 it is 2 but for k = 2 it is 7. False.
(ii) 4q² − 6q + 2q − 3 = 4q² − 4q − 3, which is odd. False.
(iii) (2m)² = 4m², and (2m + 1)² = 4m² + 4m + 1 = 4m(m + 1) + 1; m(m + 1) is even, so 4m(m + 1) is a multiple of 8. True.
(iv) 36n² + 24n + 4 − (16n² + 24n + 9) = 20n² − 5; 20n² is not a square for n = 1. False.

content.text: A number leaves a remainder of $3$ when divided by $7$, and another number leaves a remainder of $5$ when divided by $7$. What is the remainder when their sum, difference, and product are divided by $7$?
content.question: A number leaves a remainder of 3 when divided by 7, and another number leaves a remainder of 5 when divided by 7. What is the remainder when their sum, difference, and product are divided by 7?
content.question_tex: A number leaves a remainder of $3$ when divided by $7$, and another number leaves a remainder of $5$ when divided by $7$. What is the remainder when their sum, difference, and product are divided by $7$?
content.publication_text: A number leaves a remainder of $3$ when divided by $7$, and another number leaves a remainder of $5$ when divided by $7$. What is the remainder when their sum, difference, and product are divided by $7$?

content.text:
$1$. Write the numbers as $7a + 3$ and $7b + 5$.
$2$. Sum: $7a + 7b + 8 = 7(a + b + 1) + 1$, remainder $1$.
$3$. Difference: $(7b + 5) - (7a + 3) = 7(b - a) + 2$, remainder $2$; the other order leaves $5$.
$4$. Product: $49ab + 35a + 21b + 15 = 7(7ab + 5a + 3b + 2) + 1$, remainder $1$.
Answer: Sum: remainder $1$; difference: remainder $2 ($or $5$ the other way round); product: remainder $1$

content.text:
Observe the pattern in the figure below. Draw the next figure in the sequence. How many circles does it have? How many total circles are there in Step 10? Write an expression for the number of circles in Step k.
There are many ways of interpreting this pattern.
Does your method match any of these, or is it different? Each expression that we have identified appears different, but are they really different? Since they describe the same pattern, they should all be the same. Let us simplify each expression and find out.
When carried out correctly, all methods lead to the same answer; k² + 2k. The expression k² + 2k gives the number of circles at Step k of this pattern.
Use this formula to find the number of circles in Step 15.
In Mathematics, there are often multiple ways of looking at a pattern, and different ways of approaching and solving the same problem.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Step 1 has 3 circles, Step 2 has 8, Step 3 has 15. How many in Step 4?
2. See it as a square of side k + 1 with one circle missing: (k + 1)² − 1.
3. Or as a k by k square with two strips of k: k² + 2k. Or k(k + 1) + k, or a k by (k + 2) rectangle.
4. Every way simplifies to k² + 2k, so the different-looking answers are all right.

content.text:
Find the area of the (interior) shaded region in the figure below. All four rectangles have the same dimensions.
Tadang's method: The total region is a square of side (m + n) with an area (m + n)². Subtracting the area of four rectangles from the total area will give the area of the interior shaded region. That is, (m + n)² − 4mn.
Yusuf's method: The shaded region is a square with sidelength (n − m). So, its area is (n − m)².
By expanding both expressions, check that (m + n)² − 4mn = (n − m)².

content.text:
1. Predict first: four m by n rectangles surround a small square. Is its area found by adding or by taking away?
2. Tadang takes the four rectangles away from the big square: (m + n)² − 4mn.
3. Yusuf reads the side of the small square directly: n − m, so (n − m)².
4. Expand both: they are the same expression.

content.text:
Find out the area of the region with slanting lines in the figure. All three rectangles have the same dimensions.
Anusha's method: Required area = Area (ABCD) − Area (EFGH). Area of ABCD = x². Area of EFGH = xy. Required area = x² − xy.
Vaishnavi's method: QS = y + x + y = x + 2y. Area of PQSR = x (x + 2y). Required area = Area of PQSR − (area of the three rectangles) = x (x + 2y) − 3xy.
Aditya's method: The required area is 2 times the area of JKLM. JK = (x − y)/2, KM = x. Required area = 2x ((x − y)/2) = x (x − y).
By expanding the expressions, verify that all three expressions are equivalent. If x = 8 and y = 3, find the area of the shaded region.

concepts.concept_name: This Way or That Way: Q1

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S21.T21.C103.IMG1}}
$1$. One way: a square of side $k + 1$ with one circle missing, $(k + 1)^2 - 1 = k^2 + 2k + 1 - 1 = k^2 + 2k$.
$2$. Another way: a rectangle of $k$ by $k + 2$, $k(k + 2) = k^2 + 2k$.
$3$. Step $4$: $16 + 8 = 24$.
$4$. Step $10$: $100 + 20 = 120$.
$5$. Step $15$: $225 + 30 = 255$.
Answer: $k^2 + 2k$ circles; Step $4$ has $24$, Step $10$ has $120$, Step $15$ has $255$

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S21.T21.C105.IMG1}}
$1$. Step $n$ is a square of side $n + 2$ with a hole of side $n$.
$2$. $(n + 2)^2 - n^2 = n^2 + 4n + 4 - n^2 = 4n + 4$.

$4$. Step $4$: $16 + 4 = 20$. Step $10$: $40 + 4 = 44$.

$1$. Tadang: $(m + n)^2 - 4mn = m^2 + 2mn + n^2 - 4mn$.
$2$. $= m^2 - 2mn + n^2$.

$4$. Both are $m^2 - 2mn + n^2$, so the two methods agree.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S21.T21.C111.IMG1}}
$1$. Method $1$: the dashed region is a rectangle of sides $p - r$ and $s - r$, area $(p - r)(s - r)$.
$2$. Method $2$: the whole rectangle minus the two strips plus the corner removed twice: $ps - pr - sr + r^2$.
$3$. $(p - r)(s - r) = ps - pr -$ rs $+ r^2$, so both methods agree.
$4$. For $p = 6$, $r = 3.5$, $s = 9$: $(6 - 3.5)(9 - 3.5) = 2.5 \times 5.5 = 13.75$.
Answer: $(p - r)(s - r) = ps - pr - sr + r^2$; the area is $13.75$ square units

media.context: We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two statements in words are turned into expressions with a letter: two more than a square number, and the sum of the squares of two numbers that follow each other. Each option is tested by putting in a number, as the pattern expressions were.

video_script.why: The child has written an expression for a pattern and tested it with a step number, and now picks expressions for statements in words in the same way.

marks.ask: the words which expressions fit each? appear
marks.one: statement one appears with its option cards
marks.two: statement two appears with its option cards
marks.book: the small title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='one'/>Statement one is, two more than a square number.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Statement two is, the sum of the squares of two numbers, one after the other.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Each statement has a list of expressions.
Which expressions fit each statement?
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; statement one: Two more than a square number; statement two: The sum of the squares of two consecutive numbers; each with a row of option cards

marks.stop: the words which expressions fit each? glow in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the statements and cards hold still and the words which expressions fit each? glow

marks.test: k = 4 is put in and 4² + 2 × 4 = 24 appears
marks.letter: a letter k stands for any step number

narration: <bookmark mark='letter'/>A letter stands for any number, so a statement in words becomes an expression.
<bookmark mark='test'/>We test an expression by putting in a number, as we did for the circles pattern.
beats.on_screen: the circles pattern expression k² + 2k tested with k = 4: 4² + 2 × 4 = 24

marks.given: the two statements are written on the board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, two statements, each with a list of expressions.
beats.on_screen: Given: two statements, each with a list of expressions

marks.find: the thing to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to pick every expression that fits each statement.
beats.on_screen: To find: every expression that fits each statement

marks.more: two more than it, s² + 2, is written
marks.square: the square number s² is written

narration: <bookmark mark='letter'/>First, take statement one.
Let the number be s.
<bookmark mark='square'/>The square number is s squared.
<bookmark mark='more'/>Two more than it is s squared plus two.
beats.on_screen: (i) number s; square number = s²; two more = s² + 2

marks.last: the values 12 and 5 of the last two options are written and struck out
marks.rest: the values 25, 13 and 18 of three other options are written and struck out
marks.three: s = 3 is put in and the target 11 is written

beats.colours: the matching option in the accent colour, the others in the warning colour
narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Second, test the options with s as three.
The square number is nine, and two more is eleven.
<bookmark mark='fit'/>The expression s squared plus two gives eleven, so it fits.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>The square of s plus two is twenty five.
S squared plus four is thirteen, and two s squared is eighteen.
<bookmark mark='last'/>Two squared times s is twelve, and two plus s is five.
None of these is eleven.
beats.on_screen: s = 3: square number 9, two more is 11; s² + 2 = 11 ✓; (s + 2)² = 25; s² + 4 = 13; 2s² = 18; 2²s = 12; 2 + s = 5

marks.pair: the numbers m and m + 1 are written
marks.other: the pair m − 1 and m and m² + (m − 1)² are written

narration: <bookmark mark='pair'/>Third, take statement two.
Two numbers, one after the other, are m and m plus one.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>The sum of their squares is m squared plus the square of m plus one.
<bookmark mark='other'/>The pair could also be m minus one and m.
Then the sum is m squared plus the square of m minus one.
beats.on_screen: (ii) m, m + 1: m² + (m + 1)²; m − 1, m: m² + (m − 1)²

marks.big: 85 = 6² + 7² is written and struck out for the pair 3 and 4
marks.two: m² + n² is written with the words no link between m and n
marks.rest: 10 and 49 are written and struck out
marks.three: m = 3 is put in and the pair 3 and 4 is written

beats.colours: the struck out options in the warning colour
narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Fourth, test the other options with m as three, for the numbers three and four.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>M squared plus one is ten.
The square of m plus m plus one is forty nine.
<bookmark mark='big'/>The option built from two m gives eighty five, the squares of six and seven.
It fits only pairs whose smaller number is even.
<bookmark mark='two'/>M squared plus n squared has no link between m and n, so it fits nothing.
beats.on_screen: m = 3, numbers 3 and 4, target 25: m² + 1 = 10; (m + (m + 1))² = 49; (2m)² + (2m + 1)² = 85; m² + n² has no link between m and n

marks.back: the words put the answers back in the question are written
marks.plus: m = 3 gives m² + (m + 1)² = 9 + 16 = 25 and is ticked
marks.minus: m = 4 gives m² + (m − 1)² = 16 + 9 = 25 and is ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Fifth, put the answers back in the question.
The squares of three and four add to nine plus sixteen, which is twenty five.
<bookmark mark='plus'/>With m as three, the first sum is nine plus sixteen, twenty five.
<bookmark mark='minus'/>With m as four, the second sum is sixteen plus nine, twenty five again.

marks.ans: the answer s² + 2 for statement one is boxed
marks.two: m² + (m + 1)² is boxed for statement two

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Two more than a square number is s squared plus two.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The second statement gives m squared plus the square of m plus one.
<bookmark mark='three'/>It also gives m squared plus the square of m minus one.
beats.on_screen: Answer: (i) s² + 2 (ii) m² + (m + 1)² and m² + (m − 1)²

video_script.anchor: the two statements with their lists of expressions on option cards
video_script.design: One idea: write the statement with a letter, then test each option with a number. The two statements stay in the anchor band; each test sits on the working board.
source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 3)
maths_rules: (i) a square number is s²; two more than it is s² + 2
s = 3: square number 9, two more is 11; s² + 2 = 11; (s + 2)² = 25; s² + 4 = 13; 2s² = 18; 2²s = 12; 2 + s = 5; only s² + 2 gives 11
(ii) two numbers one after the other are m and m + 1, or m − 1 and m; sums of squares m² + (m + 1)² and m² + (m − 1)²
m = 3: m² + 1 = 10; (m + (m + 1))² = 7² = 49; (2m)² + (2m + 1)² = 36 + 49 = 85 = 6² + 7², the squares of 6 and 7, so it fits only pairs whose smaller number is even
m² + n² has no link between m and n
video_script.payoff_line: Two more than a square number is s squared plus two

final_answer.spoken: part one is s squared plus two; part two is m squared plus the square of m plus one, and m squared plus the square of m minus one

video_script.substitution: Write the statement with a letter, put in a number such as three, and keep only the options that give the same value.
open_questions: In part (i), 2 + s also fits if s itself is the square number; the worklist takes s as the number being squared, so only s² + 2 is kept.
In part (ii), (2m)² + (2m + 1)² is the sum of squares of two numbers that follow each other when the smaller is even; the worklist keeps only the two expressions that fit every pair.

media.description: Two numbers are added, and the sum is multiplied by half of the sum. The steps are written as an expression with letters and shown to equal half of the square of the sum, then checked with the numbers three and five.

video_script.why: The child has shown that expressions for one region are equal by working with them, and now shows that a rule given in words equals a short expression.

marks.ask: the words prove: half of the square of the sum appear
marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.cards: the number cards a and b appear

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='cards'/>Take any two numbers, and add them together.
<bookmark mark='steps'/>Then multiply this by half of the sum of the two numbers.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Write an expression for these steps.
Then prove the result is half of the square of the sum.
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; two number cards a and b; the steps: add the two numbers, then multiply by half of the sum; the words prove: half of the square of the sum

<bookmark mark='work'/>Working with the expressions showed that they were equal, as it did for the slanting region.

beats.on_screen: sum of the two numbers = a + b

narration: <bookmark mark='half'/>Second, take half of the sum, which is eigh plus b, divided by two.
<bookmark mark='mul'/>Multiply the sum by it.
The expression is eigh plus b, times, eigh plus b over two.
beats.on_screen: half of the sum = (a + b)/2; the steps give (a + b) × (a + b)/2

marks.half: (a + b)²/2 is written with the words half of the square of the sum

beats.colours: the square of the sum in the accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='square'/>Third, the sum times the sum is the square of the sum, eigh plus b all squared.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Divide by two to get eigh plus b all squared, over two.
That is half of the square of the sum.

marks.back: the words put the answer back in the question are written with a = 3 and b = 5
marks.half: the square of the sum 64 and half of 64 = 32 are written and ticked
marks.steps: sum 8, half of the sum 4 and 8 × 4 = 32 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Fourth, put the answer back in the question, and take three and five.
<bookmark mark='steps'/>Their sum is eight, and half of it is four.
Eight times four is thirty two.
<bookmark mark='half'/>The square of the sum is sixty four, and half of it is thirty two, so both agree.
beats.on_screen: put the answer back: a = 3, b = 5: sum 8, half of the sum 4, 8 × 4 = 32; square of the sum 64, half of 64 = 32

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The steps give the sum times half of the sum.
The result is half of the square of the sum.
beats.on_screen: Answer: (a + b) × (a + b)/2 = (1/2)(a + b)²

video_script.anchor: two number cards a and b, with the steps add, then multiply by half of the sum
video_script.design: One idea: write the steps once with letters, then see the sum times itself as a square. The two number cards stay in the anchor band; the working board holds each line.
source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 8)
never_show: a/2 + b as the half of the sum
maths_rules: the two numbers are a and b; their sum is a + b
half of the sum is (a + b)/2
the result is (a + b) × (a + b)/2 = (a + b)²/2 = (1/2)(a + b)²
(a + b) × (a + b) = (a + b)², the square of the sum
check with 3 and 5: sum 8, half of the sum 4, 8 × 4 = 32; square of the sum 64, half of 64 is 32
video_script.payoff_line: The result is half of the square of the sum

final_answer.spoken: the sum times half of the sum is half of the square of the sum

video_script.substitution: Write the sum with letters, write half of the sum, multiply them, and check the result with the numbers three and five.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the area that needs to be tiled.

marks.width: the pieces w, g, w of the width are added to g + 2w
marks.length: the pieces w, g, 2w, g, w of the length are added to 2g + 4w

beats.colours: the length and width pieces in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='length'/>First, find the sides of the whole park.
The length is w, g, two w, g and w added, which is two g plus four w.
<bookmark mark='width'/>The width is w plus g plus w, which is g plus two w.
beats.on_screen: length = w + g + 2w + g + w = 2g + 4w; width = w + g + w = g + 2w

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Second, multiply the length by the width.
That is two g plus four w, times g plus two w.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Two g times g is two g squared.
Two g times two w is four g w.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Four w times g is four g w.
Four w times two w is eight w squared.
<bookmark mark='join'/>The whole park is two g squared plus eight g w plus eight w squared.
beats.on_screen: whole park = (2g + 4w)(g + 2w) = 2g × g + 2g × 2w + 4w × g + 4w × 2w = 2g² + 4gw + 4gw + 8w² = 2g² + 8gw + 8w²

marks.plots: the two green plots glow and 2g² is written

narration: <bookmark mark='plots'/>Third, take away the two green plots.
Each is g squared, so two g squared come away.
<bookmark mark='left'/>What is left is eight g w plus eight w squared.
beats.on_screen: take away the two green plots: 2g² + 8gw + 8w² − 2g² = 8gw + 8w²

marks.back: the words put the answer back in the question are written with g = 3 and w = 1
marks.park: the park 10 by 5 = 50 and the plots 2 × 9 = 18 are written, then 50 − 18 = 32

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Fourth, put the answer back in the question, with g as three and w as one.
<bookmark mark='park'/>The park is ten by five, which is fifty.
Two plots of nine take away eighteen, and thirty two is left.
<bookmark mark='same'/>The expression gives eight plus twenty four, also thirty two.

marks.ans: the answer is boxed with its unit

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The area to be tiled is eight w squared plus eight g w square feet.
That is eight w times w plus g.
beats.on_screen: Answer: 8w² + 8gw sq. ft., that is 8w(w + g)

content.text:
$1$. (i): A square number is $s^2$; two more than it is $s^2 + 2$.
$2$. $(s + 2)^2$ is the square of a number two more, not two more than a square.
$3$. (ii): Two consecutive numbers are $m$ and $m + 1$, or $m - 1$ and $m$.
$4$. So $m^2 + (m + 1)^2$ and $m^2 + (m - 1)^2$ both fit; $(2m)^2 + (2m + 1)^2$ fits only some pairs.
Answer: (i): $s^2 + 2$; (ii): $m^2 + (m + 1)^2$ and $m^2 + (m - 1)^2$

content.text: What is the algebraic expression describing the following steps: add any two numbers, then multiply this by half of the sum of the two numbers? Prove that this result will be half of the square of the sum of the two numbers.

content.publication_text: What is the algebraic expression describing the following steps: add any two numbers, then multiply this by half of the sum of the two numbers? Prove that this result will be half of the square of the sum of the two numbers.

content.text:
$1$. Call the numbers $a$ and $b$; their sum is $a + b$.
$2$. Half of the sum is $\frac{a + b}{2}$.
$3$. $(a + b) \times \frac{a + b}{2} = \frac{(a + b)^2}{2}$.
$4$. That is half of the square of the sum. Check with $3$ and $5$: $8 \times 4 = 32$ and $\frac{64}{2} = 32$.
Answer: $(a + b) \times \frac{a + b}{2} = (\frac{1}{2})(a + b)^2$

content.publication_text:
A tiny park is coming up in Dhauli. Two square plots, each of area $g^2\text{ sq. ft}$., will have a green cover. All the remaining area is a walking path $w ft$. wide that needs to be tiled. Write an expression for the area that needs to be tiled.
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S22.T22.C116.IMG1}}

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S22.T22.C117.IMG1}}
$1$. The park is $w + g + 2w + g + w = 2g + 4w$ long and $w + g + w = g + 2w$ wide.
$2$. Whole park: $(2g + 4w)(g + 2w) = 2g^2 + 4gw + 4gw + 8w^2 = 2g^2 + 8gw + 8w^2$.
$3$. Take away the two plots, $2g^2$.
$4$. Area to be tiled $= 8gw + 8w^2 = 8w(g + w)$.
Answer: $8w^2 + 8gw sq$. $ft$., that is $8w(w + g)$
steps: The park is w + g + 2w + g + w = 2g + 4w long and w + g + w = g + 2w wide.
Whole park: (2g + 4w)(g + 2w) = 2g² + 4gw + 4gw + 8w² = 2g² + 8gw + 8w².
Take away the two plots, 2g².
Area to be tiled = 8gw + 8w² = 8w(g + w).

topics.summary: The product of two sums, the square of a sum, the square of a difference, the difference of two squares, many ways of seeing one pattern, and the Coin Conjoin puzzle.

content.text:
We extended the distributive property to find the product of two expressions each of which has two terms. The general form for the same is (a + b) × (c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd.
We saw some special cases of this identity. (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², (a + b) (a − b) = a² − b².
We considered different patterns, and explored how to understand them using algebra. We saw that, often, there are multiple ways to solve a problem and arrive at the same correct answer. Finding different methods to approach and solve the same problem is a creative process.

content.text:
Coin Conjoin
Arrange 10 coins in a triangle as shown in the figure below on the left. The task is to turn the triangle upside down by moving one coin at a time. How many moves are needed? What is the minimum number of moves?
A triangle of 3 coins can be inverted (turned upside down) with a single move, and a triangle of 6 coins can be inverted by moving 2 coins.
The 10-coin triangle can be flipped with just 3 moves; did you figure out how? Find out the minimum possible moves needed to flip the next bigger triangle having 15 coins. Try the same for bigger triangular numbers.
Is there a simple way to calculate the minimum number of coin moves needed for any such triangular arrangement?

3. The counts 1, 2, 3, 5 follow the number of coins divided by 3, rounded down.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the fewest moves that turn a triangle of 10 coins upside down, and then a triangle of 15 coins.
{{DIAGRAM:M5.S23.T23.C121.IMG2}}
1. For 10 coins (rows 1, 2, 3, 4), keep the middle block still and move the three corner coins: 3 moves.
2. The pattern so far: 3 coins need 1 move, 6 need 2, 10 need 3.
3. For 15 coins (rows 1 to 5), keeping the largest block still leaves 5 coins to move.
4. Each count is the number of coins divided by 3, rounded down: 3, 6, 10, 15 give 1, 2, 3, 5.
Answer: 10 coins need 3 moves and 15 coins need 5; in general the coins divided by 3, rounded down

objectives.objective_text: Students expand a(b + c) and (a + b)c with the distributive property and find the increase in 23 × 27 when either number is increased by 1.
Students expand (a + 1)(b + 1) and (a + 1)(b − 1), state the increase in each product, and explain why such equalities are called identities.
Students find pairs for which increasing one number by 1 and decreasing the other by 1 makes the product decrease, and check the identity with negative integers.
Students write the products around a middle product pq in a multiplication grid as expressions, using the distributive property to grow and shrink each factor by 1.
Students expand (a + m)(b + n) into four products, link each product to a part of the rectangle, and use it to find how a product changes when both numbers grow.
Students use the four-part product with negative changes to expand (a − 2)(b + 3), (a − 3)(b − 4) and (a ± u)(b ± v), fixing each sign by the rules of integer multiplication.
Students distribute a term over a bracket of three terms, simplify each product with exponent notation, and decide which terms are like terms that can be added.
Students expand (a + b)(a + b) and (a + b)(a² + 2ab + b²), collect like terms, and check the result with numbers.
Students multiply two sums and other brackets with numbers, letters and minus signs, collect like terms, and find a pattern in products of the form (a − b)(a + b) and (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
Students multiply a number by 11 by writing it as the number times 10 plus the number, and find the product in one line by adding neighbouring digits with carries.
Students multiply by 101 as the number times 100 plus the number, write the product in one line by adding digits two places apart, and extend the rule to 1001 and 10001.
Students multiply by 101 and 1001 in one line and multiply by 99 and 999 by subtracting the number from a hundred or a thousand times it.
Students multiply two-digit, three-digit, four-digit and seven-digit numbers by 11 in one line by adding neighbouring digits and carrying.
Students split a square of side 65 into a square of 60, a square of 5 and two rectangles of 60 by 5, and add the four areas to find 65².
Students state the square of a sum identity (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², decide when it exceeds a² + b², and expand (m + 3)², (6 + p)² and (6x + 5)².
Students expand (3j + 2k)² using the square of a sum identity and again using the distributive property, and compare the two results.
Students square 104 and 37 quickly by splitting each into two parts whose squares are easy and using the square of a sum.
Students find 55² from a square of 60 by removing two rectangles of 60 by 5 and adding back the small square of 5 that was removed twice.
Students derive (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² by the distributive property and from the square of a sum, and expand (b − 6)², (−2a + 3)² and (7y − 3/(4z))².
Students square 99 and 58 quickly by writing each as a round number minus a small number and using the square of a difference.
Students test the pattern that twice a sum of two squares is a sum of two squares and explain it by adding the square of a sum and the square of a difference.
Students prove the difference of two squares (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² by expansion and by moving a piece of a square, and use it to compute 98 × 102 and 45 × 55.
Students explain why a² = (a + b)(a − b) + b² and use it to square 31 and 197 quickly.
Students compare (a − b)² with (b − a)², express 100 as a difference of squares, square numbers with the identities, and test whether the patterns hold for negative integers and fractions.
Students check six simplifications, explain each mistake such as a forgotten term, a sign slip or a missing 2ab, and write the correct simplified expression.
Students check six more simplifications, spot unlike terms added together and missing products, and write the correct expression for each mistake.
Students decide which identity fits each product, a square of a sum, a square of a difference or a sum times a difference, and use it to compute 46², 397 × 403, 91² and 43 × 45.
Students count the circles in a growing pattern four ways, simplify each expression to k² + 2k, and find the number of circles in Step 10 and Step 15.
Students count the square tiles in a growing pattern, find the tiles in Step 4 and Step 10, and write the tiles in Step n in two ways.
Students find the area of the shaded square inside four equal rectangles by Tadang's method and Yusuf's method, and expand both expressions to show (m + n)² − 4mn = (n − m)².
Students check that Anusha's, Vaishnavi's and Aditya's expressions for the area of the region with slanting lines are equal and find the area when x = 8 and y = 3.
Students describe the area of the dashed region in two ways, simplify both expressions to the same expression, and find the area when p = 6, r = 3.5 and s = 9.
Students restate the product of two sums (a + b)(c + d), the square of a sum, the square of a difference and the difference of two squares, and recall that one pattern has many expressions.

Do this for the other 2 by 2 squares. What do you observe about the diagonal products? Explain why this happens. (Hint: label the numbers in each 2 by 2 square as a, a + 1 in the top row and a + 7, a + 8 in the bottom row.)

Book item: Verify which of the following statements are true. (i) (k + 1)(k + 2) − (k + 3) is always 2. (ii) (2q + 1)(2q − 3) is a multiple of 4. (iii) Squares of even numbers are multiples of 4, and squares of odd numbers are 1 more than multiples of 8. (iv) (6n + 2)² − (4n + 3)² is 5 less than a square number.

Book item: A number leaves a remainder of 3 when divided by 7, and another number leaves a remainder of 5 when divided by 7. What is the remainder when their sum, difference, and product are divided by 7?

Book item: Choose three consecutive numbers, square the middle one, and subtract the product of the other two. Repeat the same with other sets of numbers. What pattern do you notice? How do we write this as an algebraic equation? Expand both sides of the equation to check that it is a true identity.
Book item: Which is larger? Find out without fully computing the product. (i) 14 × 26 or 16 × 24 (ii) 25 × 75 or 26 × 74
Book item: Write the number of circles in Step k in two ways, show they agree, and find Steps 4, 10 and 15.
Book item: Write the number of circles in Step k in two ways, show they agree, and find Steps 4, 10 and 15.
Book item: The tile pattern has 8, 12 and 16 tiles in its first three steps. Find the tiles in Step 4, Step 10 and Step n.
Book item: Show that Tadang's expression (m + n)² − 4mn and Yusuf's expression (n − m)² are equal.
Book item: Verify that x² − xy, x(x + 2y) − 3xy and x(x − y) are equal, and find the area for x = 8, y = 3.

Book item: Write an expression for the area of the dashed region in the figure, a p by s rectangle with a strip of width r removed along one side and one end. Use more than one method to arrive at the answer. Substitute p = 6, r = 3.5 and s = 9, and calculate the area.

Book item: For each statement identify the appropriate algebraic expression(s). (i) Two more than a square number: 2 + s, (s + 2)², s² + 2, s² + 4, 2s², 2²s. (ii) The sum of the squares of two consecutive numbers: m² + n², (m + n)², m² + 1, m² + (m + 1)², m² + (m − 1)², (m + (m + 1))², (2m)² + (2m + 1)².

Book item: What is the algebraic expression describing the following steps: add any two numbers, then multiply this by half of the sum of the two numbers? Prove that this result will be half of the square of the sum of the two numbers.

Book item: A tiny park is coming up in Dhauli. Two square plots, each of area g² sq. ft., will have a green cover. All the remaining area is a walking path w ft. wide that needs to be tiled. Write an expression for the area that needs to be tiled.

Book item: For each of the two patterns shown, (i) draw the next figure in the sequence, (ii) find how many basic units there are in Step 10, (iii) write an expression for the number of basic units in Step y. Pattern (a) has 9, 16 and 25 units in Steps 1 to 3; pattern (b) has 5, 11 and 19.
Book item: Find the fewest moves that turn a triangle of 10 coins upside down, and then a triangle of 15 coins.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter grows out of one question: when a number in a product changes, how does the product change? A product is drawn as a rectangle of rows and columns, so splitting a side splits the rectangle, and every identity in the chapter (the product of two sums, the square of a sum or a difference, the difference of two squares) is first seen as an area and then checked by the distributive property.

points.text: Every concept opens with a prediction, such as whether (a + b)² is bigger than a² + b², and the distributive property then settles it term by term.
points.title: Predict, then expand

points.text: Rectangles split into rows and columns, a square of 65 split into four parts, and a square of 55 carved out of a square of 60 show why each identity holds.
points.title: Areas make identities visible

points.text: Fast multiplication, fast squaring and number patterns come first as arithmetic and are then explained with letter-numbers that work for every integer and fraction.
points.title: Numbers first, letters next

points.text: Ten tools, each used once: splitting a rectangle, collecting the four parts of a product of two sums, adding neighbour digits, building the square of a sum and of a difference, sliding a difference of squares, generalising a pattern, sorting expressions by identity, four rectangles in a square, and regrouping a growing pattern.
points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
